{{short description|American physicist}}

'''Stuart Samuel''' is a [[theoretical physics|theoretical physicist]] known for his work<ref name="prl03">{{Cite journal|last1=Samuel |first1=Stuart|title=On the Speed of Gravity and the '''v'''/'''c''' Corrections to the Shapiro Time Delay |journal= Phys. Rev. Lett. |year=2003 |volume= 90 |article-number=231101 | doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.90.231101 | pmid=12857246 | issue=23 | arxiv=astro-ph/0304006 | bibcode=2003PhRvL..90w1101S|s2cid=15905017}}</ref> on the [[speed of gravity]] and for his work<ref name="prd89">{{Cite journal|last1=Kostelecký |first1=V. Alan |last2=Samuel |first2=Stuart|year=1989 |title=Spontaneous breaking of Lorentz symmetry in string theory |journal=Physical Review D |publisher=APS |volume=39 |issue=2 |pages=683–685 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevD.39.683|bibcode = 1989PhRvD..39..683K |pmid=9959689 |hdl=2022/18649 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> with [[Alan Kostelecký]] on spontaneous Lorentz violation in [[string theory]], now called the [[Bumblebee models|Bumblebee model]]. He also made significant contributions in [[Field theory (physics)#Field theory|field theory]] and [[particle physics]].

Samuel graduated from [[Princeton University]] with a Bachelor of Arts in mathematics in 1975, and in 1979, he graduated from the [[UC Berkeley]], with a Doctor of Philosophy in physics. He was formerly a member of the [[Institute for Advanced Study]] at Princeton, a professor of physics at [[Columbia University]], and a professor of physics at [[City College of New York]].

== Earlier work ==

In early work, Samuel used [[Field (physics)#Field theory|particle field theory]] methods to obtain results in [[statistical mechanics]].<ref name="prd78">{{Cite journal|last1=Samuel |first1=Stuart|title= The Grand Partition Function in Field Theory with Applications to Sine-Gordon |journal= Phys. Rev. D |year=1978 |volume= 18 |issue=6|page= 1916 | doi=10.1103/PhysRevD.18.1916  |bibcode = 1978PhRvD..18.1916S }}</ref><ref name="jmp80a">{{Cite journal|last1=Samuel |first1=Stuart|title= The Use of Anticommuting Integrals in Statistical Mechanics. 1.  |journal= J. Math. Phys. |year=1980 |volume= 21 |issue=12|pages= 2806–2814  | doi=10.1063/1.524404 |bibcode = 1980JMP....21.2806S }}</ref><ref name="jmp80b">{{Cite journal|last1=Samuel |first1=Stuart|title= The Use of Anticommuting Integrals in Statistical Mechanics. 2.  |journal= J. Math. Phys. |year=1980 |volume= 21 |issue=12|page= 2815  | doi=10.1063/1.524405  |bibcode = 1980JMP....21.2815S }}</ref><ref name="jmp80c">{{Cite journal|last1=Samuel |first1=Stuart|title= The Use of Anticommuting Integrals in Statistical Mechanics. 3.  |journal= J. Math. Phys. |year=1980 |volume= 21 |issue=12|page= 2820  | doi=10.1063/1.524406|bibcode = 1980JMP....21.2820S }}</ref> In particular, Samuel uncovered a particularly simple way to solve the two-dimensional [[Ising model]]. It was shown to be equivalent to a non-interacting [[Quantum field theory|field theory]] of [[Fermions|fermionic-like particles]]. This allowed a rapid computation of the [[Partition function (statistical mechanics)|partition function]]<ref name="jmp80a"/> and [[Correlation function (statistical mechanics)|correlation functions]].<ref name="jmp80b"/> Samuel went on to treat certain interacting statistical mechanics systems using [[Perturbation theory|perturbative field theory]].<ref name="jmp80c"/>

== Scalar lattice QCD ==

In 1985, Samuel and co-worker K.J.M. Moriarty were among the first to obtain a reasonably accurate computation of the [[hadron]] mass spectrum using computer simulations of [[Lattice qcd|lattice quantum chromodynamics (QCD)]]. They overcame the difficulties that other theorists were encountering at the time by making an approximation: They replaced the [[spin 1/2]], [[fermion]]ic quarks with spin zero scalar particles and corrected for this approximation by treating the spin degrees of freedom using [[perturbation theory]]. There were three advantages to doing this: (i) [[Scalar field theory|scalar]] quarks required less computer memory, (ii) simulations using scalar [[quark]]s required less computer time, and (iii) it avoided the [[Fermion doubling| fermion doubling problem]]. Their lattice QCD computation<ref name="plb85">{{Cite journal|last1=Samuel |first1=Stuart|last2=Moriarty|first2=K.J.M.|title= Precise hadron mass calculations from lattice QCD |journal= Phys. Lett. B  |year=1985 |volume= 158  |issue=5|pages= 437–441  | doi=10.1016/0370-2693(85)90449-6 |bibcode = 1985PhLB..158..437S }}</ref> of the [[meson]] mass spectrum agreed well with the one in nature with the exception of the [[pion]] mass, where it is known that treating spin perturbatively is not a good approximation due to approximate [[Spontaneous symmetry breaking|spontaneous breaking]] of [[chiral symmetry]]. The lattice computation of the [[baryon]] spectrum was equally impressive.<ref name="plb86a">{{Cite journal|last1=Samuel |first1=Stuart|last2=Moriarty  |first2=K.J.M. |title=Precise Baryon Mass Calculations From Scalar Lattice QCD |journal= Phys. Lett. B  |year=1986 |volume=166|issue=4|pages= 413–418| doi=10.1016/0370-2693(86)91590-X|bibcode = 1986PhLB..166..413S |url=https://cds.cern.ch/record/163700}}</ref> Samuel and Moriarty went on to make mass predictions for hadrons involving the [[bottom quark]] that had not yet been produced in [[Particle accelerator|accelerators]].<ref name="plb86b">{{Cite journal|last1=Samuel |first1=Stuart|last2=Moriarty| first2 = K.J.M.| title= Beautiful Mass Predictions From Scalar Lattice QCD |journal= Phys. Lett. B  |year=1986 |volume=175|issue=2|pages= 197–201| doi= 10.1016/0370-2693(86)90715-X|bibcode = 1986PhLB..175..197S |url= https://cds.cern.ch/record/163884/files/198512010.pdf}}</ref> These predictions were later confirmed except for the one for the {{Subatomic particle| link=yes|Bottom Lambda}} baryon.<ref name="plb87">{{Cite journal|last1=Martin|first1=Andre|last2=Richard|first2=J.M.| title= Beautiful and Other Heavy Baryons Revisited |journal= Phys. Lett. B  |year=1987 |volume=185|issue=3–4|pages= 426–430| doi = 10.1016/0370-2693(87)91029-X|bibcode = 1987PhLB..185..426M |url=https://cds.cern.ch/record/173192}}</ref>

== Supersymmetry work ==

Samuel's most important work in [[supersymmetry]] arose in a collaboration with the theorist [[Julius Wess]] in a publication called "Secret Supersymmetery."<ref name="npb83">{{Cite journal|last1=Samuel |first1=Stuart|last2=Wess|first2=Julius|title=Secret Supersymmetry|journal= Nucl. Phys. B  |year=1983 |volume= 233  |issue=3|pages= 488–510  | doi = 10.1016/0550-3213(84)90580-7|bibcode = 1984NuPhB.233..488S }}</ref> In this work, the two physicists constructed an effective low-energy theory of the supersymmetric generalization of the [[Standard Model]] of particle physics for the situation in which supersymmetry is [[spontaneously broken]]. The main conclusion was: Although there may be few low-energy manifestations of spontaneously broken supersymmetry, there should be at least one charged [[Higgs field]] and two neutral Higgs fields beyond the usual neutral one of the Standard Model. All supersymmetric extensions of the Standard Model have these extra spin-0 [[boson]] particles. The important conclusion is that if additional Higgs particles are discovered in nature then it is suggestive of an underlying supersymmetric structure even if the [[Superpartner|supersymmetric partners]] of the particles in the Standard Model are not observed experimentally.

== String theory work ==

Samuel's most important contribution in [[string theory]] was the development of off-shell [[conformal field theory]].<ref name="npb88a">{{Cite journal|last1=Samuel |first1=Stuart|title= Covariant Off-shell String Amplitudes  |journal= Nucl. Phys. B  |year=1988 |volume= 308  |issue=2–3|pages= 285–316  | doi=10.1016/0550-3213(88)90566-4 |bibcode = 1988NuPhB.308..285S }}</ref><ref name="npb88b">{{Cite journal|last1=Bluhm |first1=Robert |last2=Samuel|first2=Stuart|title= Off-shell Conformal Field Theory  |journal= Nucl. Phys. B  |year=1988 |volume= 308  |issue=2 |pages= 317–360  | doi= 10.1016/0550-3213(89)90458-6 |bibcode = 1989NuPhB.325..275B }}</ref> This allowed the computation of the scattering of string states when the [[On shell and off shell|on-shell condition]] E{{sup|2}} = m{{sup|2}}c{{sup|4}} + p{{sup|2}}c{{sup|2}} is [[Analytic continuation|analytically continued]] so that it no longer holds.<ref name="npb88a"/> The [[On shell and off shell|off-shell]] extension of string [[scattering amplitude]]s was thought to be impossible because of a [[no-go theorem]].<ref name="nca74">{{Cite journal|last1=Collins|first1=PV|last2=Friedman|first2=KA|title= Off-Shell Amplitudes and Currents in the Dual Resonance Model |journal= Nuovo Cimento A  |year=1975 |volume= 28  |issue=2|pages=  173–192  | doi=10.1007/BF02820878 |bibcode = 1975NCimA..28..173C |s2cid=117078172}}</ref> However, Samuel was able to use [[Edward Witten|Witten]]'s version of [[string field theory]] to achieve this result. One of the assumptions of the "no-go" theorem was avoided (the use of an infinite number of [[Ghost (physics)|ghost states]]).

== Bosonic technicolor ==

Samuel is the creator of bosonic technicolor.<ref name="npb90">{{Cite journal|last1=Samuel |first1=Stuart|title= Bosonic Technicolor |journal= Nucl. Phys. B |year=1990 |volume= 347 |issue=3|pages= 625–650 | doi= 10.1016/0550-3213(90)90378-Q |bibcode = 1990NuPhB.347..625S }}</ref> Two approaches to solving to the [[hierarchy problem]] are [[Technicolor (physics)|technicolor]] and [[supersymmetry]]. The former has difficulties with [[flavor-changing neutral current]]s and light [[pseudo-Goldstone boson]]s, while the latter predicts [[superpartner]] particles that have not been currently observed. Bosonic technicolor is a supersymmetric version of technicolor that eliminates the difficulties that technicolor and supersymmetry have separately. In this model, the masses of superpartners can be about two orders of magnitude higher than in usual supersymmetry extensions of the standard model.

== Neutrino oscillations in dense neutrino gases ==

Because [[neutrino]]s have masses, the three flavors of neutrinos ([[electron neutrino]] {{SubatomicParticle|electron neutrino}}, [[muon neutrino]] {{SubatomicParticle|muon neutrino}} and [[tau neutrino]] {{SubatomicParticle|tau neutrino}}) change into each other and back, a phenomenon called [[neutrino oscillations]]. When one has a dense gas of neutrinos, it is not straightforward to determine how neutrino oscillations behave. This is because the oscillation of a single neutrino in the gas depends on the flavors of the neutrinos nearby, and the oscillation of the nearby neutrinos depend on the flavor of that single neutrino (and of other individual nearby neutrinos). Samuel was the first to develop a self-consistent formalism to address this.<ref name="prd93">{{Cite journal|last1=Samuel |first1=Stuart|title= Neutrino oscillations in dense neutrino gases |journal= Phys. Rev. D |year=1993 |volume= 48 |issue=4|pages= 1462–1477 | doi= 10.1103/PhysRevD.48.1462 |pmid=10016384|bibcode = 1993PhRvD..48.1462S }}</ref> He observed a number of interesting phenomena that can occur in such systems including a self-induced [[Mikheyev–Smirnov–Wolfenstein effect]] and a [[Parametric oscillator#Parametric resonance|parametric resonant]] conversion.

Samuel and colleague [[Alan Kostelecký]] have used Samuel's formalism to analyze neutrino oscillations in the [[Early universe#Early universe|early universe]].<ref name="prd94">{{Cite journal|last1=Kostelecký |first1=Alan |last2=Samuel |first2=Stuart|title= Nonlinear neutrino oscillations in the expanding universe |journal= Phys. Rev. D |year=1994 |volume= 49 |issue=4 |pages=  1740–1757 | doi= 10.1103/PhysRevD.49.1740 |pmid=10017160 |bibcode = 1994PhRvD..49.1740K |hdl=2022/18663 |url=https://scholarworks.iu.edu/dspace/bitstream/2022/18663/1/PhysRevD.49.1740.pdf |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

== Awards and prizes ==

Samuel has received a number of awards for his research including a Control Data Corporation PACER Award (with Dr. K. M. Moriarty) for outstanding computer programming, an [[Alexander von Humboldt Foundation|Alexander von Humboldt Fellowship]], and the Chester–Davis Prize (from Indiana University). He was one of 90 scientists in 1984 to be honored as an [[Alfred P. Sloan Foundation|Alfred P. Sloan Research Recipient]].<ref name="sc">{{Cite news|title=90 Receive Sloan Foundation Grants|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1984/03/11/nyregion/90-receive-sloan-foundation-grants.html|date=11 March 1984|newspaper=The New York Times}}</ref>
